questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How chefs create new flavours for their restaurants
Two sisters whose senses mix, so words have tastes
Why some people cannot taste or smell anything
How to choose healthy food when you feel hungry
questions.why: Sam says they'll meet two sisters from Glasgow who can 'taste' every word they hear.

questions.q: What do Neil and Sam say about their favourite things?
options: They both love the taste of coffee most
Neil loves lavender; Sam loves the colour green
Neither of them has a favourite word
Neil likes saying 'nincompoop'; Sam loves coffee
questions.why: Neil mentions green, sweet-and-sour and the word 'nincompoop'; Sam mentions coffee, lavender and bread.

questions.q: What does Jen taste when she hears her daughter's name, Sophia?
options: Pink marshmallows
Noodles
A tuna baguette
Rotten eggs
questions.why: Neil says when Jen hears 'Sophia', she tastes pink marshmallows.

questions.q: How many different types of synaesthesia could there be?
options: Only two or three
Exactly five, one for each sense
Up to 150
More than 4,000
questions.why: Sam says there could be as many as 150 different types of synaesthesia.

questions.q: Why does Jen compare her synaesthesia to being pregnant?
options: Because it started when she was pregnant
Because it makes her feel tired and sick
Because her doctor thought she was pregnant
Words can make her badly want certain foods
questions.why: She says a word that tastes like tuna makes her want a tuna baguette – 'almost like… having a craving'.

questions.q: According to Guy Leschziner, what has research shown about synaesthesia?
options: It is only caused by an overactive imagination
It has a real basis in the brain and in genes
It usually disappears when people get older
It is much more common in men than in women
questions.why: He says it was dismissed in the past, but it has 'an underlying neurological and genetic basis'.

questions.q: Who else in the sisters' family has synaesthesia?
options: Jen's daughter
Their brothers
Their parents
Nobody else
questions.why: Neil says Julie and Jen's brothers don't have it, but Jen's daughter does.

questions.q: About how many people in the world have some form of sense mixing?
options: Fewer than one in a thousand
About half of all people
About 4%
Around 15%
questions.why: Neil says an estimated 4% of the world population have some form of sense mixing.
